pages.text: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland

image.note: Cover: Alice and the White Rabbit, a small door

pages.text: Contents. Down the Rabbit-Hole / A Pool of Tears / A Grinning Cat / A Mad Tea-Party / The Queen's Croquet / The Trial.

Alice was bored, sitting by the river with nothing to do, when a White Rabbit ran past, muttering and looking at its pocket-watch. A rabbit with a waistcoat and a watch! Alice jumped up and ran after it, and tumbled straight into the strangest adventure ever dreamed.

image.note: Alice spotting the hurrying White Rabbit

pages.text: Down went the Rabbit into a large hole under the hedge, and down, without a moment's thought, went Alice after it. The hole dropped straight, then suddenly opened wide, and Alice found herself falling, slowly, ever so slowly, down and down and down.

image.note: Alice falling down the rabbit-hole

pages.text: She fell so slowly that she had time to look about. The walls were lined with cupboards and shelves and pictures. She took a jar marked MARMALADE off a shelf as she passed, found it empty, and put it back on another shelf, still falling. "After a fall like this," she thought, "stairs will seem nothing at all."

image.note: Alice drifting past shelves as she falls

pages.text: At last she landed, softly, in a long hall lined with locked doors. Behind a curtain she found one tiny door, and beyond it the loveliest garden she ever saw. But the door was far too small to fit through, and she could only kneel and peep.

image.note: Alice peering through a tiny door

pages.text: On a glass table sat a little bottle labelled DRINK ME. Alice checked it was not marked poison, and then drank. At once she began to shrink, smaller and smaller, until she was just the right size for the door. But now the key was up on the table, far out of reach.

image.note: Alice shrinking beside the tiny door

pages.text: Then she found a cake marked EAT ME, and ate it, hoping to grow tall enough to reach the key. Grow she did, but far too much. Up shot Alice, taller than the room, her head against the ceiling, one giant eye at the tiny door. "Curiouser and curiouser!" she cried, forgetting her grammar entirely.

image.note: Giant Alice cramped in the hall

pages.text: Being nine feet tall and unable to reach the garden was too much, and Alice began to cry, great giant tears that ran across the floor. Then, fanning herself with the Rabbit's dropped fan, she shrank again, so fast she nearly vanished, and splashed straight into the pool of her own tears.

image.note: Tiny Alice swimming in a pool of tears

pages.text: She was not alone. A Mouse swam by, and a Duck, and a Dodo, and all sorts of creatures who had fallen in too. They swam to shore, a soggy, grumbling crowd, and to get dry the Dodo declared a very odd race with no clear start and no clear end, and everybody won a prize. Alice began to feel she rather liked it here.

image.note: Soggy animals on the shore with the Dodo

pages.text: Wandering on, Alice met a large blue Caterpillar sitting on a mushroom, asking dreamy, rude questions. "Who are you?" it demanded. "I hardly know, sir," said Alice, "I have changed size so many times today." The Caterpillar told her one side of the mushroom would make her taller, and the other, smaller.

image.note: Alice and the blue Caterpillar on a mushroom

pages.text: So Alice nibbled the mushroom, this side and that, until she could make herself any size she pleased. Feeling clever, she set off again, and soon met the oddest creature yet: a large cat, grinning from ear to ear, sitting up in a tree.

image.note: The Cheshire Cat grinning in a tree

pages.text: "I'm the Cheshire Cat," it said, "and we're all mad here. You're mad. I'm mad." "How do you know I'm mad?" asked Alice. "You must be," said the Cat, "or you wouldn't have come here." And then, slowly, it began to vanish, tail first, until nothing was left but its grin, hanging alone in the air.

image.note: The Cat vanishing, only its grin left

pages.text: The Cat had pointed the way to the March Hare, and there, at a long table under a tree, Alice found the maddest tea-party in the world. A March Hare and a Mad Hatter squashed a sleepy Dormouse between them, and all three cried, "No room! No room!" though the table was nearly empty.

image.note: The mad tea-party under a tree

pages.text: "Have some wine," said the Hare. There was no wine. "Why is a raven like a writing-desk?" asked the Hatter, and would not answer his own riddle. It was always six o'clock, they said, and so always tea-time, and they never washed the cups but only moved round to the next clean place.

image.note: Alice puzzling at the endless tea-party

pages.text: It was the silliest, rudest party Alice had ever known, all riddles with no answers and talk with no sense. At last she grew quite cross with the muddle of it, got up, and walked off into the wood. "That is the stupidest tea-party I ever was at in all my life," she said.

image.note: Alice leaving the tea-party, cross

pages.text: Deeper in, Alice came to a garden where playing-card gardeners were painting white roses red, in a terrible panic. "The Queen ordered red," they whispered, "and we planted white by mistake. If she sees, it's off with our heads!" And just then a great procession marched in, and the Queen of Hearts herself.

image.note: Card gardeners painting the roses red

pages.text: The Queen was a fierce, red-faced lady who shouted "Off with his head!" at the smallest thing, over and over, at almost everyone. Nobody was ever really harmed, for the King quietly pardoned them all behind her back, but oh, how she loved to shout it.

image.note: The furious Queen of Hearts shouting

pages.text: Then came a game of croquet, the strangest ever played. The balls were live hedgehogs, curled up. The mallets were live flamingos, who kept twisting their necks round to look at Alice just as she swung. The hoops were card-soldiers, who wandered off whenever they liked. No one could possibly win.

image.note: Croquet with flamingo mallets and hedgehog balls

pages.text: At last there was a great trial. The Knave of Hearts was accused of stealing the Queen's jam tarts, and the whole pack of cards crowded in to judge him. The evidence was nonsense, the witnesses were madder still, and the Queen kept demanding the verdict before the trial had even begun.

image.note: The courtroom of playing cards

pages.text: "Sentence first, verdict afterwards!" cried the Queen. "That's not how it works at all," said Alice, who had been growing all through the trial and was now quite her full size again. "Who cares for you?" she said boldly. "You're nothing but a pack of cards!"

image.note: Full-size Alice standing up to the cards

pages.text: At that the whole pack rose into the air and came fluttering down upon her. Alice gave a little scream, and beat them off, and woke. She was lying on the riverbank, her sister beside her, dry leaves fluttering onto her face. It had all, every mad moment of it, been a dream.

image.note: Alice waking on the riverbank

pages.text: "Oh, I've had such a curious dream!" said Alice, and she ran off to tea, thinking, as the sun went down, what a wonderful, nonsensical place Wonderland had been. And perhaps, if you ever chase a hurrying rabbit, you might tumble down and find it too.

image.note: Alice running home at sunset, remembering

pages.text: Wonderland friends. The White Rabbit, always late. The blue Caterpillar, full of questions. The Cheshire Cat, who grins and vanishes. The Mad Hatter, at his endless tea. The Queen of Hearts, who loves to shout. A whole world of glorious nonsense, waiting behind a very small door.

image.note: Montage of Wonderland characters
